11	knitr::opts_chunk$set(
12	  collapse = TRUE,
13	  comment = "#>"
14	)
15	```
16	
17	`CellTFusion` integrates immune cell type deconvolution with transcription factor (TF)–gene regulatory networks to characterize immune cell states in the tumor microenvironment (TME) from bulk RNA-seq data.
18	
19	Starting from a count matrix, `CellTFusion` builds **cell groups** — sets of deconvolution features related to the same TF co-activity module to the same degree (a similar correlation with the module activity) — and scores them in each sample. The cell group scores can be tested against clinical variables and used as features for machine learning, and they are summarized into **latent factors**, a compact representation of the TME described by their cell niches (the cell groups that contribute most to each factor).
20	
21	## Installation
22	
23	To avoid GitHub API rate limit issues, set up a Personal Access Token (PAT) before installing:
24	
25	```{r, eval = FALSE}
26	# install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))
27	usethis::create_github_token()
28	gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
29	```
30	
31	Install `CellTFusion` from GitHub:
32	
33	```{r, eval = FALSE}
34	# install.packages("pak")
35	pak::pkg_install("VeraPancaldiLab/CellTFusion")
36	```
37	
38	## Quick start
39	
40	The `CellTFusion()` wrapper runs the whole pipeline in one call, using the example data shipped with the package. Intermediate results and plots are saved in a `Results/` folder in the working directory.
41	
42	```{r, eval = FALSE}
43	library(CellTFusion)
44	
45	res <- CellTFusion(
46	  raw_counts     = CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto,
47	  normalized     = TRUE,
48	  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
49	  file_name      = "Tutorial"
50	)
51	
52	head(res$Latent_spaces$Z)  # latent factor scores (samples x factors)
53	```
54	
55	## Pipeline
56	
57	| Step | Function | Tutorial |
58	| --- | --- | --- |
59	| Cell type deconvolution | `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
60	| TF activity inference | `compute.TFs.activity()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
61	| TF co-activity modules | `compute.WTCNA()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
62	| Pathway activity | `compute.pathway.activity()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
63	| Cell groups | `construct_cell_groups()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
64	| Latent factors | `compute.latent_factors()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
65	| Cell niches | `compute_cells_niches()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
66	| Clinical associations | `scores.stat.analysis()` | [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html) |
67	| Survival analysis | `compute.survival.analysis()` | [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html) |
68	| Cross-validation with `pipeML` | `prepare_celltfusion_folds()` | [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html) |
69	| Projection of new cohorts | `compute.test.set()` (cell groups), `project_factors()` (latent factors) | [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html) |
70	| Multi-cohort analysis | `CellTFusion(batch = ...)` | [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html) |
71	
72	## Tutorials
73	
74	Step-by-step tutorials are available in the **Articles** section of the navigation bar:
75	
76	- **[Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html)** — cell type deconvolution, TF activity, TF co-activity modules and pathway activity
77	- **[Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html)** — build cell groups, extract latent factors and characterize cell niches
78	- **[Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html)** — associations with clinical variables and survival
79	- **[Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html)** — use cell group scores as features and score independent cohorts
80	- **[Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)** — correct for cohort effects with `batch`
81	
82	## Shiny app
83	
84	`CellTFusion` includes an interactive app to run the pipeline on the example data or on your own data:
85	
86	```{r, eval = FALSE}
87	shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny", package = "CellTFusion"))
88	```
89	
90	## Citation
91	
92	If you use `CellTFusion` in a scientific publication, please cite:
93	
94	> Hurtado, M., & Pancaldi, V. (2026). *CellTFusion: A transcriptional regulatory network framework for the identification of functional multicellular states from bulk RNA-seq data.* bioRxiv. <https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.06.30.735682>

---
title: "CellTFusion"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{CellTFusion}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

`CellTFusion` integrates immune cell type deconvolution with transcription factor (TF)–gene regulatory networks to characterize immune cell states in the tumor microenvironment (TME) from bulk RNA-seq data.

Starting from a count matrix, `CellTFusion` builds **cell groups** — sets of deconvolution features related to the same TF co-activity module to the same degree (a similar correlation with the module activity) — and scores them in each sample. The cell group scores can be tested against clinical variables and used as features for machine learning, and they are summarized into **latent factors**, a compact representation of the TME described by their cell niches (the cell groups that contribute most to each factor).

## Installation

To avoid GitHub API rate limit issues, set up a Personal Access Token (PAT) before installing:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))
usethis::create_github_token()
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

Install `CellTFusion` from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("VeraPancaldiLab/CellTFusion")
```

## Quick start

The `CellTFusion()` wrapper runs the whole pipeline in one call, using the example data shipped with the package. Intermediate results and plots are saved in a `Results/` folder in the working directory.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(CellTFusion)

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts     = CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto,
  normalized     = TRUE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
  file_name      = "Tutorial"
)

head(res$Latent_spaces$Z)  # latent factor scores (samples x factors)
```

## Pipeline

| Step | Function | Tutorial |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cell type deconvolution | `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
| TF activity inference | `compute.TFs.activity()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
| TF co-activity modules | `compute.WTCNA()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
| Pathway activity | `compute.pathway.activity()` | [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) |
| Cell groups | `construct_cell_groups()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
| Latent factors | `compute.latent_factors()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
| Cell niches | `compute_cells_niches()` | [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html) |
| Clinical associations | `scores.stat.analysis()` | [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html) |
| Survival analysis | `compute.survival.analysis()` | [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html) |
| Cross-validation with `pipeML` | `prepare_celltfusion_folds()` | [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html) |
| Projection of new cohorts | `compute.test.set()` (cell groups), `project_factors()` (latent factors) | [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html) |
| Multi-cohort analysis | `CellTFusion(batch = ...)` | [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html) |

## Tutorials

Step-by-step tutorials are available in the **Articles** section of the navigation bar:

- **[Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html)** — cell type deconvolution, TF activity, TF co-activity modules and pathway activity
- **[Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html)** — build cell groups, extract latent factors and characterize cell niches
- **[Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html)** — associations with clinical variables and survival
- **[Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html)** — use cell group scores as features and score independent cohorts
- **[Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)** — correct for cohort effects with `batch`

## Shiny app

`CellTFusion` includes an interactive app to run the pipeline on the example data or on your own data:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny", package = "CellTFusion"))
```

# CellTFusion

`CellTFusion` integrates immune cell type deconvolution with
transcription factor (TF)–gene regulatory networks to characterize
immune cell states in the tumor microenvironment (TME) from bulk RNA-seq
data.

Starting from a count matrix, `CellTFusion` builds **cell groups** —
sets of deconvolution features whose abundance follows the activity of a
TF co-activity module — and summarizes them into **latent factors**, a
compact representation of the TME that can be annotated as TME states,
tested against clinical variables and used as features for machine
learning.

## Installation

To avoid GitHub API rate limit issues, set up a Personal Access Token
(PAT) before installing:

``` r
# install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))
usethis::create_github_token()
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

Install `CellTFusion` from GitHub:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("VeraPancaldiLab/CellTFusion")
```

## Quick start

The
[`CellTFusion()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/CellTFusion.md)
wrapper runs the whole pipeline in one call, using the example data
shipped with the package. Intermediate results and plots are saved in a
`Results/` folder in the working directory.

``` r
library(CellTFusion)

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw.counts     = CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto,
  normalized     = TRUE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
  cancer_type    = "skcm",
  file_name      = "Tutorial"
)

head(res$Latent_spaces$Z)  # latent factor scores (samples x factors)
res$TME_states             # mapping of each latent factor to a TCGA meta-program
```

## Pipeline

| Step                           | Function                                                                                                                     | Tutorial                                                                                                    |
|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cell type deconvolution        | [`multideconv::compute.deconvolution()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/multideconv/reference/compute.deconvolution.html) | [Feature computation](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a1_feature_computation.md)     |
| TF activity inference          | [`compute.TFs.activity()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute.TFs.activity.md)                  | [Feature computation](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a1_feature_computation.md)     |
| TF co-activity modules         | [`compute.WTCNA()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute.WTCNA.md)                                | [Feature computation](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a1_feature_computation.md)     |
| Pathway activity               | [`compute.pathway.activity()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute.pathway.activity.md)          | [Feature computation](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a1_feature_computation.md)     |
| Cell groups                    | [`construct_cell_groups()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/construct_cell_groups.md)                | [Cell groups and latent factors](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a2_cell_groups.md)  |
| Latent factors                 | [`compute.latent_factors()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute.latent_factors.md)              | [Cell groups and latent factors](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a2_cell_groups.md)  |
| Cell niches                    | [`compute_cells_niches()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute_cells_niches.md)                  | [Cell groups and latent factors](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a2_cell_groups.md)  |
| Hallmark GSEA per factor       | [`compute_factor_gsea()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute_factor_gsea.md)                    | [TME state characterization](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a3_tme_states.md)       |
| Meta-program mapping           | [`map_factors_to_metaprograms()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/map_factors_to_metaprograms.md)    | [TME state characterization](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a3_tme_states.md)       |
| TME subtype annotation         | [`map_factors_to_TME()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/map_factors_to_TME.md)                      | [TME state characterization](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a3_tme_states.md)       |
| Clinical associations          | [`scores.stat.analysis()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/scores.stat.analysis.md)                  | [Statistical analysis](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a4_statistical_analysis.md)   |
| Survival analysis              | [`compute.survival.analysis()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/compute.survival.analysis.md)        | [Statistical analysis](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a4_statistical_analysis.md)   |
| Cross-validation with `pipeML` | [`prepare_celltfusion_folds()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/prepare_celltfusion_folds.md)        | [Machine learning workflows](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a5_machine_learning.md) |
| Projection of new cohorts      | [`project_test_factors()`](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/reference/project_test_factors.md)                  | [Machine learning workflows](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a5_machine_learning.md) |
| Multi-cohort analysis          | `CellTFusion(batch = TRUE)`                                                                                                  | [Multi-cohort analysis](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a6_batch_analysis.md)        |

## Tutorials

Step-by-step tutorials are available in the **Articles** section of the
navigation bar:

- **[Feature
  computation](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a1_feature_computation.md)**
  — cell type deconvolution, TF activity, TF co-activity modules and
  pathway activity
- **[Cell groups and latent
  factors](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a2_cell_groups.md)**
  — build cell groups, extract latent factors and characterize cell
  niches
- **[TME state
  characterization](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a3_tme_states.md)**
  — Hallmark GSEA, TCGA meta-programs and TME subtypes
- **[Statistical
  analysis](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a4_statistical_analysis.md)**
  — associations with clinical variables and survival
- **[Machine learning
  workflows](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a5_machine_learning.md)**
  — use latent factors as features and project independent cohorts
- **[Multi-cohort
  analysis](https://verapancaldilab.github.io/CellTFusion/articles/a6_batch_analysis.md)**
  — correct for cohort effects with `batch = TRUE`

## Shiny app

`CellTFusion` includes an interactive app to run the pipeline on the
example data or on your own data:

``` r
shiny::runApp(system.file("shiny", package = "CellTFusion"))
```

## Citation

If you use `CellTFusion` in a scientific publication, please cite:

> Hurtado, M., & Pancaldi, V. (2026). *CellTFusion: A transcriptional
> regulatory network framework for the identification of functional
> multicellular states from bulk RNA-seq data.* bioRxiv.
> <https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.06.30.735682>

1	---
2	title: "Feature computation"
3	output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
4	vignette: >
5	  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Feature computation}
6	  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
7	  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
8	bibliography: references.bib
9	link-citations: yes
10	---
11	
12	```{r, include = FALSE}
13	knitr::opts_chunk$set(
14	  collapse = TRUE,
15	  comment = "#>"
16	)
17	```
18	
19	```{r setup}
20	library(CellTFusion)
21	```
22	
23	`CellTFusion` combines two families of features computed from bulk RNA-seq data: **cell type deconvolution** and **transcription factor (TF) activity**, the latter summarized into TF co-activity modules. Pathway activities are computed alongside. This tutorial runs each step on its own, with its key arguments and outputs. All of them are run automatically, in this order, by the `CellTFusion()` wrapper (see [Running the full pipeline](#running-the-full-pipeline)).
24	
25	Load the example data:
26	
27	```{r}
28	raw.counts <- CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto
29	traitdata  <- CellTFusion::traitdata.tuto
30	```
31	
32	## **Normalization**
33	
34	TF and pathway activities are computed from log2-transformed TPM values. Deconvolution methods use TPM without the log transform; this is handled internally by `compute.deconvolution()`. If your data are already TPM-normalized (and not log-transformed), use `normalized = FALSE` in `CellTFusion()`: the TPM values are then used as they are for deconvolution and log2(TPM + 1) is computed internally for the other steps.
35	
36	```{r, eval = FALSE}
37	counts.norm <- data.frame(ADImpute::NormalizeTPM(raw.counts, log = TRUE))
38	```
39	
40	## **Cell type deconvolution**
41	
42	Cell type proportions are estimated with `compute.deconvolution()` from the companion package [`multideconv`](https://github.com/VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv), which runs several deconvolution methods (Quantiseq, Epidish, DeconRNASeq, DWLS and CIBERSORTx) with multiple signatures. The result is a matrix of samples x method-signature-cell type features.
43	
44	Key arguments:
45	
46	- `raw.counts` — count matrix (genes x samples).
47	- `methods` — deconvolution methods to run.
48	- `normalized` — whether to TPM-normalize the counts before deconvolution.
49	- `credentials.mail` / `credentials.token` — CIBERSORTx credentials, only needed if `"CBSX"` is in `methods`.
50	- `return` — if `TRUE`, saves the matrix in `Results/`.
51	
52	```{r, eval = FALSE}
53	deconv <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution(
54	  raw.counts,
55	  methods    = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
56	  normalized = TRUE,
57	  return     = FALSE
58	)
59	```
60	
61	## **TF activity**
62	
63	`compute.TFs.activity()` infers the activity of each TF in each sample from the expression of its targets, using `decoupleR` [@10.1093/bioadv/vbac016] and a TF-target network (regulon). By default the univariate linear model is used (`method = "ulm"`); `"mlm"`, `"wsum"` and `"consensus"` (the consensus of the three) are also available.
64	
65	Key arguments:
66	
67	- `counts_norm` — log-normalized expression matrix (genes x samples), typically log2(TPM + 1).
68	- `TF.collection` — source of the regulon:
69	  - `"CollecTRI"` (default) [@10.1093/nar/gkad841], fetched from OmnipathR, and `"Dorothea"` (confidence levels A and B, from the `dorothea` package) are curated regulons. Each collection is cached in its own file in `Results/` (`TF_target_collection_<collection>.csv`) and reused in later runs.
70	  - `"ARACNE"` uses a **data-driven, cohort-specific** network inferred with ARACNe [@Margolin2006], which derives TF-target edges from the mutual information between expression profiles across a cohort and removes indirect interactions. This is useful for a large, homogeneous cohort in which curated interactions may not hold. The network is read from `input/ARACNE/<cancer_type>/network/network.txt` (relative to the working directory), a tab-separated file with `Regulator` and `Target` columns and a `mor` column with the sign of each interaction (1 activation, -1 repression). The sign should be computed once, as the sign of the Spearman correlation between the TF and its target in the cohort used to build the network. If the file has no `mor` column, the signs are computed from the samples given to `compute.TFs.activity()` and a warning is given: they then depend on these samples and can differ between cohorts or between a training and a test set.
71	- `min_targets_size` — minimum number of targets per regulon; TFs with fewer targets are dropped (default 5).
72	- `universe` — optional user-supplied regulon (data frame with `source`, `target` and `mor` columns, all three required; `mor` is 1 for activation and -1 for repression), used instead of fetching one.
73	- `scale` — if `TRUE` (default), z-scores TF activities across samples. The scaled scores of a sample depend on the other samples of the call; use `scale = FALSE` to compare scores computed in separate calls.
74	
75	```{r, eval = FALSE}
76	tfs <- compute.TFs.activity(
77	  counts_norm       = counts.norm,
78	  TF.collection    = "CollecTRI",
79	  min_targets_size = 5,
80	  return           = TRUE
81	)
82	```
83	
84	To use your own regulon:
85	
86	```{r, eval = FALSE}
87	universe <- decoupleR::get_collectri(organism = "human", split_complexes = FALSE)
88	tfs <- compute.TFs.activity(counts.norm, universe = universe)
89	```
90	
91	To use a cohort-specific ARACNe network:
92	
93	```{r, eval = FALSE}
94	tfs_aracne <- compute.TFs.activity(
95	  counts_norm    = counts.norm,
96	  TF.collection = "ARACNE",
97	  cancer_type   = "skcm"   # reads input/ARACNE/skcm/network/network.txt
98	)
99	```
100	
101	## **TF co-activity modules**
102	
103	`compute.WTCNA()` groups TFs with similar activity patterns into **modules** using Weighted TF Co-activity Network Analysis (WTCNA), an adaptation of WGCNA [@langfelder2008wgcna] to TF activities. Each module is summarized by one score per sample, its eigengene.
104	
105	Key arguments:
106	
107	- `tfs` — TF activity matrix (samples x TFs); with `batch` (cohort of each sample), the TF activities of all the cohorts (see [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)).
108	- `network_type` — `"signed"` (default) or `"unsigned"`. In a signed network, TFs with negatively correlated activities are not connected.
109	- `clustering_method` — linkage of the hierarchical clustering of the TFs on their TOM dissimilarity; `"ward.D2"` by default (WGCNA uses `"average"`, which joins two groups of TFs according to the average dissimilarity between their TFs).
110	- `min_module_size` — minimum number of TFs per module. TFs that fit no module (grey) are left out, with a message.
111	- `corr_mod` — correlation (of type `corr_type`) above which module eigengenes are merged, in single- and multi-cohort mode.
112	- `corr_type` — `"spearman"` (default) or `"pearson"`, in single- and multi-cohort mode.
113	
114	```{r, eval = FALSE}
115	network <- compute.WTCNA(
116	  tfs        = tfs,
117	  network_type      = "signed",
118	  clustering_method = "average",
119	  min_module_size            = 15,
120	  corr_mod          = 0.9,
121	  return            = TRUE
122	)
123	```
124	
125	With `return = TRUE`, diagnostic plots are saved in `Results/`. First, the scale-free topology fit used to choose the soft-thresholding power:
126	
127	```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Scale-free topology model fit versus soft-thresholding power"}
128	knitr::include_graphics("figures/soft_threshold.png")
129	```
130	
131	Then the TF dendrogram with module colors, before and after merging highly correlated modules:
132	
133	```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "48%", fig.show = "hold", fig.alt = c("TF dendrogram with module colors before merging", "TF dendrogram with module colors after merging")}
134	knitr::include_graphics(c(
135	  "figures/gene_dendrogram_before_merging.png",
136	  "figures/gene_dendrogram_after_merging.png"
137	))
138	```
139	
140	`network[[1]]` (`"TFs module matrix"`) contains the module scores (samples x modules) used to build cell groups.
141	
142	## **Pathway activity**
143	
144	`compute.pathway.activity()` estimates pathway activities with `decoupleR` [@10.1093/bioadv/vbac016] and the PROGENy pathway footprints [@Schubert2018], by default with the univariate linear model (`method = "ulm"`, as in `compute.TFs.activity()`). If a list of gene sets is given, GSVA scores are computed as well.
145	
146	Key arguments:
147	
148	- `counts_norm` — log-normalized expression matrix, e.g. log2(TPM + 1) (genes x samples).
149	- `gene_sets` — optional named list of gene sets; if provided, GSVA scores are returned in addition to PROGENy.
150	- `paths` — optional custom PROGENy-style table (`source`, `target`, `weight`); by default the human PROGENy model is used.
151	- `scale` — z-score each pathway across the samples (default). The scaled scores of a sample depend on the other samples of the call; use `scale = FALSE` to compare scores computed in separate calls.
152	
153	```{r, eval = FALSE}
154	pathways <- compute.pathway.activity(
155	  counts_norm = counts.norm,
156	  return  = TRUE
157	)
158	```
159	
160	The result is a samples x pathways matrix (14 PROGENy pathways by default). Clustering it gives an overview of which pathways co-vary across the cohort:
161	
162	```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "80%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Heatmap of PROGENy pathway activities clustered by sample and pathway"}
163	knitr::include_graphics("figures/pathway_heatmap.png")
164	```
165	
166	## **Reduction of deconvolution features**
167	
168	Deconvolution features from different methods and signatures are often highly correlated. `compute.deconvolution.analysis()` from `multideconv` groups correlated features of the same cell type into **subgroups**, reducing redundancy before building cell groups.
169	
170	Key arguments:
171	
172	- `deconvolution` — output of `compute.deconvolution()`.
173	- `corr` — minimum correlation to group features into a subgroup.
174	- `corr_type` — `"spearman"` (default) or `"pearson"`.
175	- `batch` — optional cohort vector; correlations then control for cohort (see [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)).
176	
177	```{r, eval = FALSE}
178	dt <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis(
179	  deconvolution = deconv,
180	  corr          = 0.7,
181	  return        = FALSE
182	)
183	```
184	
185	## **Running the full pipeline**
186	
187	`CellTFusion()` runs all the steps above, then builds cell groups, latent factors and cell niches:
188	
189	```{r, eval = FALSE}
190	res <- CellTFusion(
191	  raw_counts     = raw.counts,
192	  normalized     = TRUE,
193	  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
194	  TF.collection  = "CollecTRI",
195	  corr           = 0.7,
196	  corr_mod       = 0.9,
197	  pval           = 0.05,
198	  file_name      = "Tutorial",
199	  return         = TRUE
200	)
201	```
202	
203	A few defaults worth knowing:
204	
205	- `deconv_methods` runs Quantiseq, CIBERSORTx (`"CBSX"`), Epidish, DeconRNASeq and DWLS by default. CIBERSORTx is only run when `cbsx_mail` and `cbsx_token` are given; without them it is skipped with a message.
206	- `cancer_type` is only used with `TF.collection = "ARACNE"`, to locate the ARACNe network.
207	- Precomputed `deconv`, `dt`, `tfs` and `pathways` can be passed to skip the corresponding steps (see [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html)).
208	
209	`res` contains every intermediate object: `$Deconvolution`, `$TFs_matrix`, `$TF_network`, `$Pathways_scores`, `$Processed_deconvolution`, `$Cell_groups`, `$Latent_spaces` and `$Cells_niches`.
210	
211	Next: [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html).
212	
213	## References

---
title: "Feature computation"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Feature computation}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
bibliography: references.bib
link-citations: yes
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(CellTFusion)
```

`CellTFusion` combines two families of features computed from bulk RNA-seq data: **cell type deconvolution** and **transcription factor (TF) activity**, the latter summarized into TF co-activity modules. Pathway activities are computed alongside. This tutorial runs each step on its own, with its key arguments and outputs. All of them are run automatically, in this order, by the `CellTFusion()` wrapper (see [Running the full pipeline](#running-the-full-pipeline)).

Load the example data:

```{r}
raw.counts <- CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto
traitdata  <- CellTFusion::traitdata.tuto
```

## **Normalization**

TF and pathway activities are computed from log2-transformed TPM values. Deconvolution methods use TPM without the log transform; this is handled internally by `compute.deconvolution()`. If your data are already TPM-normalized (and not log-transformed), use `normalized = FALSE` in `CellTFusion()`: the TPM values are then used as they are for deconvolution and log2(TPM + 1) is computed internally for the other steps.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
counts.norm <- data.frame(ADImpute::NormalizeTPM(raw.counts, log = TRUE))
```

## **Cell type deconvolution**

Cell type proportions are estimated with `compute.deconvolution()` from the companion package [`multideconv`](https://github.com/VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv), which runs several deconvolution methods (Quantiseq, Epidish, DeconRNASeq, DWLS and CIBERSORTx) with multiple signatures. The result is a matrix of samples x method-signature-cell type features.

Key arguments:

- `raw.counts` — count matrix (genes x samples).
- `methods` — deconvolution methods to run.
- `normalized` — whether to TPM-normalize the counts before deconvolution.
- `credentials.mail` / `credentials.token` — CIBERSORTx credentials, only needed if `"CBSX"` is in `methods`.
- `return` — if `TRUE`, saves the matrix in `Results/`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
deconv <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution(
  raw.counts,
  methods    = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
  normalized = TRUE,
  return     = FALSE
)
```

## **TF activity**

`compute.TFs.activity()` infers the activity of each TF in each sample from the expression of its targets, using `decoupleR` [@10.1093/bioadv/vbac016] and a TF-target network (regulon). By default the univariate linear model is used (`method = "ulm"`); `"mlm"`, `"wsum"` and `"consensus"` (the consensus of the three) are also available.

Key arguments:

- `counts_norm` — log-normalized expression matrix (genes x samples), typically log2(TPM + 1).
- `TF.collection` — source of the regulon:
  - `"CollecTRI"` (default) [@10.1093/nar/gkad841], fetched from OmnipathR, and `"Dorothea"` (confidence levels A and B, from the `dorothea` package) are curated regulons. Each collection is cached in its own file in `Results/` (`TF_target_collection_<collection>.csv`) and reused in later runs.
  - `"ARACNE"` uses a **data-driven, cohort-specific** network inferred with ARACNe [@Margolin2006], which derives TF-target edges from the mutual information between expression profiles across a cohort and removes indirect interactions. This is useful for a large, homogeneous cohort in which curated interactions may not hold. The network is read from `input/ARACNE/<cancer_type>/network/network.txt` (relative to the working directory), a tab-separated file with `Regulator` and `Target` columns and a `mor` column with the sign of each interaction (1 activation, -1 repression). The sign should be computed once, as the sign of the Spearman correlation between the TF and its target in the cohort used to build the network. If the file has no `mor` column, the signs are computed from the samples given to `compute.TFs.activity()` and a warning is given: they then depend on these samples and can differ between cohorts or between a training and a test set.
- `min_targets_size` — minimum number of targets per regulon; TFs with fewer targets are dropped (default 5).
- `universe` — optional user-supplied regulon (data frame with `source`, `target` and `mor` columns, all three required; `mor` is 1 for activation and -1 for repression), used instead of fetching one.
- `scale` — if `TRUE` (default), z-scores TF activities across samples. The scaled scores of a sample depend on the other samples of the call; use `scale = FALSE` to compare scores computed in separate calls.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tfs <- compute.TFs.activity(
  counts_norm       = counts.norm,
  TF.collection    = "CollecTRI",
  min_targets_size = 5,
  return           = TRUE
)
```

To use your own regulon:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
universe <- decoupleR::get_collectri(organism = "human", split_complexes = FALSE)
tfs <- compute.TFs.activity(counts.norm, universe = universe)
```

To use a cohort-specific ARACNe network:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tfs_aracne <- compute.TFs.activity(
  counts_norm    = counts.norm,
  TF.collection = "ARACNE",
  cancer_type   = "skcm"   # reads input/ARACNE/skcm/network/network.txt
)
```

## **TF co-activity modules**

`compute.WTCNA()` groups TFs with similar activity patterns into **modules** using Weighted TF Co-activity Network Analysis (WTCNA), an adaptation of WGCNA [@langfelder2008wgcna] to TF activities. Each module is summarized by one score per sample, its eigengene.

Key arguments:

- `tfs` — TF activity matrix (samples x TFs); with `batch` (cohort of each sample), the TF activities of all the cohorts (see [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)).
- `network_type` — `"signed"` (default) or `"unsigned"`. In a signed network, TFs with negatively correlated activities are not connected.
- `clustering_method` — linkage of the hierarchical clustering of the TFs on their TOM dissimilarity; `"ward.D2"` by default (WGCNA uses `"average"`, which joins two groups of TFs according to the average dissimilarity between their TFs).
- `min_module_size` — minimum number of TFs per module. TFs that fit no module (grey) are left out, with a message.
- `corr_mod` — correlation (of type `corr_type`) above which module eigengenes are merged, in single- and multi-cohort mode.
- `corr_type` — `"spearman"` (default) or `"pearson"`, in single- and multi-cohort mode.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
network <- compute.WTCNA(
  tfs        = tfs,
  network_type      = "signed",
  clustering_method = "average",
  min_module_size            = 15,
  corr_mod          = 0.9,
  return            = TRUE
)
```

With `return = TRUE`, diagnostic plots are saved in `Results/`. First, the scale-free topology fit used to choose the soft-thresholding power:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Scale-free topology model fit versus soft-thresholding power"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/soft_threshold.png")
```

Then the TF dendrogram with module colors, before and after merging highly correlated modules:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "48%", fig.show = "hold", fig.alt = c("TF dendrogram with module colors before merging", "TF dendrogram with module colors after merging")}
knitr::include_graphics(c(
  "figures/gene_dendrogram_before_merging.png",
  "figures/gene_dendrogram_after_merging.png"
))
```

`network[[1]]` (`"TFs module matrix"`) contains the module scores (samples x modules) used to build cell groups.

## **Pathway activity**

`compute.pathway.activity()` estimates pathway activities with `decoupleR` [@10.1093/bioadv/vbac016] and the PROGENy pathway footprints [@Schubert2018], by default with the univariate linear model (`method = "ulm"`, as in `compute.TFs.activity()`). If a list of gene sets is given, GSVA scores are computed as well.

Key arguments:

- `counts_norm` — log-normalized expression matrix, e.g. log2(TPM + 1) (genes x samples).
- `gene_sets` — optional named list of gene sets; if provided, GSVA scores are returned in addition to PROGENy.
- `paths` — optional custom PROGENy-style table (`source`, `target`, `weight`); by default the human PROGENy model is used.
- `scale` — z-score each pathway across the samples (default). The scaled scores of a sample depend on the other samples of the call; use `scale = FALSE` to compare scores computed in separate calls.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pathways <- compute.pathway.activity(
  counts_norm = counts.norm,
  return  = TRUE
)
```

The result is a samples x pathways matrix (14 PROGENy pathways by default). Clustering it gives an overview of which pathways co-vary across the cohort:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "80%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Heatmap of PROGENy pathway activities clustered by sample and pathway"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/pathway_heatmap.png")
```

## **Reduction of deconvolution features**

Deconvolution features from different methods and signatures are often highly correlated. `compute.deconvolution.analysis()` from `multideconv` groups correlated features of the same cell type into **subgroups**, reducing redundancy before building cell groups.

Key arguments:

- `deconvolution` — output of `compute.deconvolution()`.
- `corr` — minimum correlation to group features into a subgroup.
- `corr_type` — `"spearman"` (default) or `"pearson"`.
- `batch` — optional cohort vector; correlations then control for cohort (see [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
dt <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis(
  deconvolution = deconv,
  corr          = 0.7,
  return        = FALSE
)
```

## **Running the full pipeline**

`CellTFusion()` runs all the steps above, then builds cell groups, latent factors and cell niches:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts     = raw.counts,
  normalized     = TRUE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish"),
  TF.collection  = "CollecTRI",
  corr           = 0.7,
  corr_mod       = 0.9,
  pval           = 0.05,
  file_name      = "Tutorial",
  return         = TRUE
)
```

A few defaults worth knowing:

- `deconv_methods` runs Quantiseq, CIBERSORTx (`"CBSX"`), Epidish, DeconRNASeq and DWLS by default. CIBERSORTx is only run when `cbsx_mail` and `cbsx_token` are given; without them it is skipped with a message.
- `cancer_type` is only used with `TF.collection = "ARACNE"`, to locate the ARACNe network.
- Precomputed `deconv`, `dt`, `tfs` and `pathways` can be passed to skip the corresponding steps (see [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html)).

`res` contains every intermediate object: `$Deconvolution`, `$TFs_matrix`, `$TF_network`, `$Pathways_scores`, `$Processed_deconvolution`, `$Cell_groups`, `$Latent_spaces` and `$Cells_niches`.

Next: [Cell groups and latent factors](a2_cell_groups.html).

## References

1	---
2	title: "Cell groups and latent factors"
3	output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
4	vignette: >
5	  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Cell groups and latent factors}
6	  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
7	  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
8	---
9	
10	```{r, include = FALSE}
11	knitr::opts_chunk$set(
12	  collapse = TRUE,
13	  comment = "#>"
14	)
15	```
16	
17	```{r setup}
18	library(CellTFusion)
19	```
20	
21	This tutorial covers the core steps of `CellTFusion`: building cell groups from TF modules and deconvolution features, extracting latent factors and characterizing cell niches. It uses two objects from the [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) tutorial:
22	
23	- `network` — TF co-activity modules from `compute.WTCNA()`.
24	- `dt` — deconvolution subgroups from `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()`.
25	
26	## **Cell groups**
27	
28	`construct_cell_groups()` correlates each TF module with the deconvolution features, clusters the significantly correlated features of each module, and cuts the dendrograms into **cell groups**. Features are clustered on the value of their correlation with the module, so a cell group is a set of features with a similar biological activity: features related to the same TF module to the same degree, which do not need to vary together across samples. Each cell group covers a single range of correlation values: the dendrogram is cut with a dynamic tree cut, clusters made of separated ranges are split, and pieces smaller than `min_cluster_size` are joined to the neighbouring group with the closest correlation. Each cell group gets a composite score per sample: the first canonical component of a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) between the group's deconvolution features and the score of its TF module, i.e. the combination of the features that correlates most with the module score. The score is oriented to be aligned with the TF module: a positive score means that the sample is on the active side of the module for that cell group, a negative score that it is on the inactive side.
29	
30	Key arguments:
31	
32	- `network`, `dt` — the inputs above.
33	- `batch` — optional cohort vector (see [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)).
34	- `pval` — p-value threshold to select the deconvolution features significantly correlated with each module.
35	- `file_name` / `return` — with `return = TRUE` (default), the colored dendrograms are saved to `Results/Dendrogram_color_clusters_<file_name>.pdf`, and the composition and the scores of the cell groups to `Results/Cell.groups.composition_<file_name>.csv` and `Results/Cell.groups.scores_<file_name>.csv`.
36	
37	```{r, eval = FALSE}
38	cell_groups <- construct_cell_groups(
39	  network           = network,
40	  dt                = dt,
41	  pval              = 0.05,
42	  clustering_method = "ward.D2",
43	  file_name         = "Tutorial"
44	)
45	```
46	
47	One dendrogram is drawn per TF module, showing how its correlated deconvolution features cluster into cell groups. The leaves are drawn in the order of their correlation with the module as far as the tree allows, and the groups are numbered from the lowest to the highest correlation. The number written next to each group is the one in the cell group name (`Dendrogram_<module>_group_<number>`); a group that the tree splits into two places is drawn, and numbered, in both. Features that are not assigned to any cluster are not part of any cell group:
48	
49	```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Dendrogram of deconvolution features clustered into cell groups for one TF module"}
50	knitr::include_graphics("figures/cell_groups_dendrogram_02.png")
51	```
52	
53	`construct_cell_groups()` returns a named list:
54	
55	| Element | Description |
56	| ------- | ----------- |
57	| `Cell_groups` | Data frame of composite scores (samples x cell groups) |
58	| `Composition` | Deconvolution features in each cell group |
59	| `Weights` | CCA projection parameters of each group (`xcoef`, `train_means`, `train_sds`; only `xcoef` with `batch`), used to score new samples |
60	
61	### Re-running with precomputed features
62	
63	`CellTFusion()` accepts precomputed `dt`, `tfs` and `pathways`, for example from a previous run (`res$Processed_deconvolution`, `res$TFs_matrix`, `res$Pathways_scores`). The corresponding steps are then skipped, which is useful to try different module or cell group parameters without recomputing the features:
64	
65	```{r, eval = FALSE}
66	res_rerun <- CellTFusion(
67	  raw_counts = raw.counts,
68	  normalized = TRUE,
69	  dt         = res$Processed_deconvolution,
70	  tfs        = res$TFs_matrix,
71	  pathways   = res$Pathways_scores,
72	  corr_mod   = 0.8,    # e.g. merge modules more readily than the default 0.9
73	  min_module_size     = 10,
74	  pval       = 0.05,
75	  return     = TRUE
76	)
77	```
78	
79	## **Latent factors**
80	
81	`compute.latent_factors()` decomposes the cell group scores into non-negative latent factors with NMF. Only the positive part of each score is used, `max(score, 0)`: how far the sample is on the active side of the group's TF module (negative scores become 0), so the factors describe the high-activity direction of the cell groups. If `rank = NULL`, the number of factors is chosen among `ranks` (2 to 15 by default, never more than the number of cell groups) with bootstrap NMF: for each rank, NMF is fitted on all the patients and on `n_boot` (100) bootstrap samples of the patients, and the factors of each run are matched to the reference factors by the cosine similarity of their profiles (their weights on the cell groups). Each factor gets its recovery frequency (proportion of runs in which it is found, similarity >= `similarity_thresh`) and its mean similarity; a factor is robust when both pass the thresholds (`recovery_thresh = 0.7` and `similarity_thresh = 0.8` by default, starting points rather than universal cutoffs). Two factors of the same rank with very similar profiles are flagged as redundant. The selected rank is the largest one whose factors are all robust and none redundant: as many factors as the data support reliably (low ranks capture the dominant patterns and are almost always stable, so the smallest stable rank would favour 2). `rank_selection` reports every candidate rank and `stability` the factors of the selected one; when two adjacent ranks are similarly good, check whether the main factors persist at the neighbouring rank.
82	
83	```{r, eval = FALSE}
84	latent_spaces <- compute.latent_factors(
85	  scores    = cell_groups$Cell_groups,
86	  rank      = NULL,
87	  seed      = 123,
88	  file_name = "Tutorial",
89	  return    = TRUE
90	)
91	
92	head(latent_spaces$Z)          # samples x factors
93	latent_spaces$rank_selection   # stability and redundancy of each candidate rank
94	latent_spaces$stability        # recovery and mean similarity of each factor
95	```
96	
97	With `return = TRUE`, the stability of each candidate rank is plotted (`Results/NMF_rank_stability_<file_name>.pdf`, followed by a page with the recovery and mean similarity of each factor of the selected rank). On the tutorial data, ranks 2 to 5 have all their factors robust and none redundant, and stability drops from rank 6, so 5 factors are kept:
98	
99	```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "95%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Lowest recovery, lowest mean similarity and highest similarity between factors of each candidate NMF rank, with the thresholds and the selected rank"}
100	knitr::include_graphics("figures/nmf_rank_stability.png")
101	```
102	
103	The result contains `Z` (factor scores, samples x factors — the input for statistics), `W` (weights of each cell group in each factor), `nmf_input` (the positive part of the scores), the NMF model, the per-sample factor proportions and the stability tables. The NMF approximates the transposed input as `W %*% diag(d) %*% t(Z)`: each column of `W` and each column of `Z` sums to 1, and the size of each factor is in `nmf_model$d`. Tests on one factor at a time do not depend on this scaling; the factor proportions of each sample (`Z` multiplied by `d`, divided by its sum per sample) take the sizes into account. `project_factors()` projects the cell group scores of new samples (from `compute.test.set()`) onto the factors, on the scale of `Z`. With `return = TRUE`, the mixture of factors in each sample is plotted:
104	
105	```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "90%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Stacked bar plot of latent factor proportions per sample"}
106	knitr::include_graphics("figures/nmf_patient_mixture.png")
107	```
108	
109	## **Cell niches**
110	
111	`compute_cells_niches()` characterizes each latent factor by the cell groups that contribute most to it: the `top_n` cell groups with the highest weight in the factor (`W`), described by their deconvolution features and the CCA coefficients of these features in the cell group scores. The deconvolution features are kept as they are (subgroups are not expanded into their members).
112	
113	```{r, eval = FALSE}
114	cells_niches <- compute_cells_niches(
115	  latent_factors = latent_spaces,
116	  cell_groups    = cell_groups,
117	  top_n          = 5,
118	  return         = TRUE,
119	  file_name      = "Tutorial"
120	)
121	```
122	
123	The result has one row per factor, cell group and feature (`factor`, `cell_group`, `module`, `weight`, `feature`, `coefficient`). For each factor, a tree network is saved (one page per factor): the factor on the left, its top cell groups in the middle (coloured by their TF module) and their features listed on the right. Edges are the CCA coefficients: red when the feature is higher in samples where the cell group is active, blue when it is lower; coefficients close to zero are thin. Features correlated with each other (e.g. several estimates of the same cell type) share their weight, so a single small edge with the opposite colour of its cell group should be read together with the rest of the group.
124	
125	```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "80%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Tree network of the top cell groups of latent factor 1 and their deconvolution features"}
126	knitr::include_graphics("figures/niche_network_factor1.png")
127	```
128	
129	A heatmap shows the NMF weights of all the cell groups in all factors (cell groups ordered by the factor where their weight is highest; outlined: the top cell groups of each factor), so that cell groups shared between factors can be seen:
130	
131	```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "60%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Heatmap of the NMF weights of all the cell groups in each latent factor, with the top cell groups of each factor outlined"}
132	knitr::include_graphics("figures/niche_weights_heatmap.png")
133	```
134	
135	## **Next steps**
136	
137	With the cell group scores and the latent factors you can:
138	
139	- test associations with clinical variables — [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html);
140	- use the cell group scores as features for prediction — [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html).

---
title: "Cell groups and latent factors"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Cell groups and latent factors}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(CellTFusion)
```

This tutorial covers the core steps of `CellTFusion`: building cell groups from TF modules and deconvolution features, extracting latent factors and characterizing cell niches. It uses two objects from the [Feature computation](a1_feature_computation.html) tutorial:

- `network` — TF co-activity modules from `compute.WTCNA()`.
- `dt` — deconvolution subgroups from `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()`.

## **Cell groups**

`construct_cell_groups()` correlates each TF module with the deconvolution features, clusters the significantly correlated features of each module, and cuts the dendrograms into **cell groups**. Features are clustered on the value of their correlation with the module, so a cell group is a set of features with a similar biological activity: features related to the same TF module to the same degree, which do not need to vary together across samples. Each cell group covers a single range of correlation values: the dendrogram is cut with a dynamic tree cut, clusters made of separated ranges are split, and pieces smaller than `min_cluster_size` are joined to the neighbouring group with the closest correlation. Each cell group gets a composite score per sample: the first canonical component of a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) between the group's deconvolution features and the score of its TF module, i.e. the combination of the features that correlates most with the module score. The score is oriented to be aligned with the TF module: a positive score means that the sample is on the active side of the module for that cell group, a negative score that it is on the inactive side.

Key arguments:

- `network`, `dt` — the inputs above.
- `batch` — optional cohort vector (see [Multi-cohort analysis](a6_batch_analysis.html)).
- `pval` — p-value threshold to select the deconvolution features significantly correlated with each module.
- `file_name` / `return` — with `return = TRUE` (default), the colored dendrograms are saved to `Results/Dendrogram_color_clusters_<file_name>.pdf`, and the composition and the scores of the cell groups to `Results/Cell.groups.composition_<file_name>.csv` and `Results/Cell.groups.scores_<file_name>.csv`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cell_groups <- construct_cell_groups(
  network           = network,
  dt                = dt,
  pval              = 0.05,
  clustering_method = "ward.D2",
  file_name         = "Tutorial"
)
```

One dendrogram is drawn per TF module, showing how its correlated deconvolution features cluster into cell groups. The leaves are drawn in the order of their correlation with the module as far as the tree allows, and the groups are numbered from the lowest to the highest correlation. The number written next to each group is the one in the cell group name (`Dendrogram_<module>_group_<number>`); a group that the tree splits into two places is drawn, and numbered, in both. Features that are not assigned to any cluster are not part of any cell group:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Dendrogram of deconvolution features clustered into cell groups for one TF module"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/cell_groups_dendrogram_02.png")
```

`construct_cell_groups()` returns a named list:

| Element | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| `Cell_groups` | Data frame of composite scores (samples x cell groups) |
| `Composition` | Deconvolution features in each cell group |
| `Weights` | CCA projection parameters of each group (`xcoef`, `train_means`, `train_sds`; only `xcoef` with `batch`), used to score new samples |

### Re-running with precomputed features

`CellTFusion()` accepts precomputed `dt`, `tfs` and `pathways`, for example from a previous run (`res$Processed_deconvolution`, `res$TFs_matrix`, `res$Pathways_scores`). The corresponding steps are then skipped, which is useful to try different module or cell group parameters without recomputing the features:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res_rerun <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts = raw.counts,
  normalized = TRUE,
  dt         = res$Processed_deconvolution,
  tfs        = res$TFs_matrix,
  pathways   = res$Pathways_scores,
  corr_mod   = 0.8,    # e.g. merge modules more readily than the default 0.9
  min_module_size     = 10,
  pval       = 0.05,
  return     = TRUE
)
```

## **Latent factors**

`compute.latent_factors()` decomposes the cell group scores into non-negative latent factors with NMF. Only the positive part of each score is used, `max(score, 0)`: how far the sample is on the active side of the group's TF module (negative scores become 0), so the factors describe the high-activity direction of the cell groups. If `rank = NULL`, the number of factors is chosen among `ranks` (2 to 15 by default, never more than the number of cell groups) with bootstrap NMF: for each rank, NMF is fitted on all the patients and on `n_boot` (100) bootstrap samples of the patients, and the factors of each run are matched to the reference factors by the cosine similarity of their profiles (their weights on the cell groups). Each factor gets its recovery frequency (proportion of runs in which it is found, similarity >= `similarity_thresh`) and its mean similarity; a factor is robust when both pass the thresholds (`recovery_thresh = 0.7` and `similarity_thresh = 0.8` by default, starting points rather than universal cutoffs). Two factors of the same rank with very similar profiles are flagged as redundant. The selected rank is the largest one whose factors are all robust and none redundant: as many factors as the data support reliably (low ranks capture the dominant patterns and are almost always stable, so the smallest stable rank would favour 2). `rank_selection` reports every candidate rank and `stability` the factors of the selected one; when two adjacent ranks are similarly good, check whether the main factors persist at the neighbouring rank.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
latent_spaces <- compute.latent_factors(
  scores    = cell_groups$Cell_groups,
  rank      = NULL,
  seed      = 123,
  file_name = "Tutorial",
  return    = TRUE
)

head(latent_spaces$Z)          # samples x factors
latent_spaces$rank_selection   # stability and redundancy of each candidate rank
latent_spaces$stability        # recovery and mean similarity of each factor
```

With `return = TRUE`, the stability of each candidate rank is plotted (`Results/NMF_rank_stability_<file_name>.pdf`, followed by a page with the recovery and mean similarity of each factor of the selected rank). On the tutorial data, ranks 2 to 5 have all their factors robust and none redundant, and stability drops from rank 6, so 5 factors are kept:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "95%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Lowest recovery, lowest mean similarity and highest similarity between factors of each candidate NMF rank, with the thresholds and the selected rank"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/nmf_rank_stability.png")
```

The result contains `Z` (factor scores, samples x factors — the input for statistics), `W` (weights of each cell group in each factor), `nmf_input` (the positive part of the scores), the NMF model, the per-sample factor proportions and the stability tables. The NMF approximates the transposed input as `W %*% diag(d) %*% t(Z)`: each column of `W` and each column of `Z` sums to 1, and the size of each factor is in `nmf_model$d`. Tests on one factor at a time do not depend on this scaling; the factor proportions of each sample (`Z` multiplied by `d`, divided by its sum per sample) take the sizes into account. `project_factors()` projects the cell group scores of new samples (from `compute.test.set()`) onto the factors, on the scale of `Z`. With `return = TRUE`, the mixture of factors in each sample is plotted:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "90%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Stacked bar plot of latent factor proportions per sample"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/nmf_patient_mixture.png")
```

## **Cell niches**

`compute_cells_niches()` characterizes each latent factor by the cell groups that contribute most to it: the `top_n` cell groups with the highest weight in the factor (`W`), described by their deconvolution features and the CCA coefficients of these features in the cell group scores. The deconvolution features are kept as they are (subgroups are not expanded into their members).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cells_niches <- compute_cells_niches(
  latent_factors = latent_spaces,
  cell_groups    = cell_groups,
  top_n          = 5,
  return         = TRUE,
  file_name      = "Tutorial"
)
```

The result has one row per factor, cell group and feature (`factor`, `cell_group`, `module`, `weight`, `feature`, `coefficient`). For each factor, a tree network is saved (one page per factor): the factor on the left, its top cell groups in the middle (coloured by their TF module) and their features listed on the right. Edges are the CCA coefficients: red when the feature is higher in samples where the cell group is active, blue when it is lower; coefficients close to zero are thin. Features correlated with each other (e.g. several estimates of the same cell type) share their weight, so a single small edge with the opposite colour of its cell group should be read together with the rest of the group.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "80%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Tree network of the top cell groups of latent factor 1 and their deconvolution features"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/niche_network_factor1.png")
```

A heatmap shows the NMF weights of all the cell groups in all factors (cell groups ordered by the factor where their weight is highest; outlined: the top cell groups of each factor), so that cell groups shared between factors can be seen:

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "60%", fig.align = "center", fig.alt = "Heatmap of the NMF weights of all the cell groups in each latent factor, with the top cell groups of each factor outlined"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/niche_weights_heatmap.png")
```

## **Next steps**

With the cell group scores and the latent factors you can:

- test associations with clinical variables — [Statistical analysis](a4_statistical_analysis.html);
- use the cell group scores as features for prediction — [Machine learning workflows](a5_machine_learning.html).

1	---
2	title: "Statistical analysis"
3	output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
4	vignette: >
5	  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Statistical analysis}
6	  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
7	  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
8	---
9	
10	```{r, include = FALSE}
11	knitr::opts_chunk$set(
12	  collapse = TRUE,
13	  comment = "#>"
14	)
15	```
16	
17	```{r setup}
18	library(CellTFusion)
19	```
20	
21	This tutorial shows how to test associations between `CellTFusion` features — latent factors, TF modules or cell groups — and clinical variables. It uses the result of `CellTFusion()`:
22	
23	```{r, eval = FALSE}
24	raw.counts <- CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto
25	traitdata  <- CellTFusion::traitdata.tuto
26	
27	res <- CellTFusion(
28	  raw_counts  = raw.counts,
29	  normalized  = TRUE,
30	  return      = TRUE
31	)
32	```
33	
34	## **Latent factors and clinical traits**
35	
36	`scores.stat.analysis()` tests each latent factor against a clinical variable and saves a plot for every significant association in `Results/`. `scores` can be the output of `compute.latent_factors()` (`res$Latent_spaces`), a samples x features matrix, or a list whose first element is that matrix (e.g. `res$Cell_groups`). The samples are matched to the rows of `coldata` by row name (without row names in `coldata`, its rows must be in the order of the scores), and samples with a missing trait are left out. The trait must be categorical.
37	
38	Available tests (`test`):
39	
40	- `"wilcox"` — Wilcoxon rank-sum test (two groups).
41	- `"ttest"` — Welch's t-test (two groups, unequal variances).
42	- `"kruskal"` — Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn post-hoc tests (two or more groups).
43	- `"anova"` — one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc tests (two or more groups).
44	- `"fisher"` — Fisher's exact test, with scores split at the median into High/Low.
45	
46	```{r, eval = FALSE}
47	sig_factors <- scores.stat.analysis(
48	  scores  = res$Latent_spaces,
49	  coldata = traitdata,
50	  trait   = "Best.Confirmed.Overall.Response",
51	  test    = "wilcox",
52	  pval    = 0.05
53	)
54	```
55	
56	The result keeps only the significant features (its first element has no column if none is significant), and its element `Statistics` gives the test of every feature (statistic, p-value, adjusted p-value). Use `padj = TRUE` to correct the p-values for the number of features tested (Benjamini-Hochberg); it is `FALSE` by default. The individual tests (`scores.wilcox.test()`, `scores.ttest()`, `scores.kruskal.test()`, `scores.anova.test()`, `scores.fisher.test()`) can also be called directly with a list whose first element is the score matrix.
57	
58	The factor scores themselves are in `res$Latent_spaces$Z`:
59	
60	```{r, eval = FALSE}
61	factor_scores <- data.frame(res$Latent_spaces$Z)
62	head(factor_scores)
63	```
64	
65	## **TF modules and clinical traits**
66	
67	`compute.metadata.association()` relates TF module scores to all clinical variables at once. The rows of `coldata` must be the same samples, in the same order, as the rows of the module matrix (an error is raised otherwise):
68	
69	- **Numeric traits** are correlated with each module (Spearman by default, `corr_type = "pearson"` for Pearson) and shown in a heatmap, annotated for p-values at or below `pval`. For traits with missing values, each p-value uses the number of samples with both values. Numeric columns are treated as continuous: convert number-coded categories (e.g. a stage coded 1 to 4) to factor to test them as groups.
70	- **Categorical traits** (text, factor and TRUE/FALSE columns) are tested with one-way ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc tests when `plot_grid = TRUE`, and saved as boxplot grids with one panel per significant module.
71	
72	Traits that cannot be tested are skipped with a message: numeric traits without variation, and categorical traits with a single level or with one value per sample (e.g. a sample identifier). Use `padj = TRUE` to correct the p-values for multiple testing across the modules, for each trait (Benjamini-Hochberg).
73	
74	```{r, eval = FALSE}
75	assoc <- compute.metadata.association(
76	  scores = res$TF_network[[1]],
77	  coldata     = traitdata,
78	  pval        = 0.05,
79	  file_name   = "Tutorial",
80	  plot_grid   = TRUE
81	)
82	
83	assoc$correlation  # module-trait correlations (numeric traits)
84	assoc$p_value      # their p-values
85	assoc$anova        # ANOVA of every module for every categorical trait
86	```
87	
88	## **TF modules and pathways**
89	
90	`compute.modules.relationship()` correlates two matrices of continuous features over the same samples, for example TF modules and pathway activities (Spearman by default, `corr_type = "pearson"` for Pearson), and saves a heatmap of the significant correlations. It is for numeric variables only; use `compute.metadata.association()` for categorical ones. With `plot_grid = TRUE`, a scatter plot is also drawn for the significant pairs (the 100 strongest at most).
91	
92	```{r, eval = FALSE}
93	rel <- compute.modules.relationship(
94	  matA      = res$TF_network[[1]],
95	  matB      = res$Pathways_scores,
96	  file_name = "Pathways_vs_TF_modules"
97	)
98	
99	rel$correlation  # correlations (TF modules x pathways)
100	rel$p_value      # their p-values
101	rel$significant  # for each TF module, the pathways significantly correlated with it
102	```
103	
104	## **Survival analysis**
105	
106	`compute.survival.analysis()` compares Kaplan-Meier survival curves with a log-rank test (packages `survival`, `survminer` and `gridExtra`). It works in two modes:
107	
108	1. **Predefined groups** (`group_column`) — e.g. a clinical risk group or a cluster assignment in the clinical data. Samples without a value for `group_column` are left out.
109	2. **Feature screening** (`scores`) — e.g. `res$Latent_spaces$Z`. Each feature is split into High/Low at a quantile (`quantile_cutoff`), and the features with a significant log-rank test (`pval`, optionally corrected with `padj = TRUE`) are returned, with a `Statistics` table giving the test of every feature. The rows of `scores` must be the same samples, in the same order, as the rows of the clinical data.
110	
111	Both modes need a time-to-event column and an event column (1 = event, 0 = censored) in the clinical data. The tutorial `traitdata` includes the overall survival of the patients: `os` (months) and `censOS` (1 = death, 0 = censored).
112	
113	```{r, eval = FALSE}
114	# Predefined groups
115	surv_group <- compute.survival.analysis(
116	  coldata       = traitdata,
117	  time_column   = "os",
118	  event_column  = "censOS",
119	  group_column  = "Best.Confirmed.Overall.Response",
120	  file_name     = "Tutorial"
121	)
122	
123	surv_group$p_value     # log-rank p-value
124	surv_group$median_PFS  # median survival per group (column name kept from the function output)
125	```
126	
127	```{r, eval = FALSE}
128	# Feature screening on latent factors
129	surv_factors <- compute.survival.analysis(
130	  coldata       = traitdata,
131	  time_column   = "os",
132	  event_column  = "censOS",
133	  scores        = res$Latent_spaces$Z,
134	  pval          = 0.05,
135	  quantile_cutoff = 0.5,   # median split; e.g. 0.75 for top quartile vs rest
136	  file_name     = "Tutorial"
137	)
138	```
139	
140	A Kaplan-Meier plot with a risk table is saved (always for predefined groups, and for every significant feature in feature screening) to `Results/SurvPlot_<group-or-feature>_<file_name>.svg` (`Results/SurvPlot_<group-or-feature>.svg` without `file_name`).

---
title: "Statistical analysis"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Statistical analysis}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(CellTFusion)
```

This tutorial shows how to test associations between `CellTFusion` features — latent factors, TF modules or cell groups — and clinical variables. It uses the result of `CellTFusion()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
raw.counts <- CellTFusion::raw.counts.tuto
traitdata  <- CellTFusion::traitdata.tuto

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts  = raw.counts,
  normalized  = TRUE,
  return      = TRUE
)
```

## **Latent factors and clinical traits**

`scores.stat.analysis()` tests each latent factor against a clinical variable and saves a plot for every significant association in `Results/`. `scores` can be the output of `compute.latent_factors()` (`res$Latent_spaces`), a samples x features matrix, or a list whose first element is that matrix (e.g. `res$Cell_groups`). The samples are matched to the rows of `coldata` by row name (without row names in `coldata`, its rows must be in the order of the scores), and samples with a missing trait are left out. The trait must be categorical.

Available tests (`test`):

- `"wilcox"` — Wilcoxon rank-sum test (two groups).
- `"ttest"` — Welch's t-test (two groups, unequal variances).
- `"kruskal"` — Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn post-hoc tests (two or more groups).
- `"anova"` — one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc tests (two or more groups).
- `"fisher"` — Fisher's exact test, with scores split at the median into High/Low.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sig_factors <- scores.stat.analysis(
  scores  = res$Latent_spaces,
  coldata = traitdata,
  trait   = "Best.Confirmed.Overall.Response",
  test    = "wilcox",
  pval    = 0.05
)
```

The result keeps only the significant features (its first element has no column if none is significant), and its element `Statistics` gives the test of every feature (statistic, p-value, adjusted p-value). Use `padj = TRUE` to correct the p-values for the number of features tested (Benjamini-Hochberg); it is `FALSE` by default. The individual tests (`scores.wilcox.test()`, `scores.ttest()`, `scores.kruskal.test()`, `scores.anova.test()`, `scores.fisher.test()`) can also be called directly with a list whose first element is the score matrix.

The factor scores themselves are in `res$Latent_spaces$Z`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
factor_scores <- data.frame(res$Latent_spaces$Z)
head(factor_scores)
```

## **TF modules and clinical traits**

`compute.metadata.association()` relates TF module scores to all clinical variables at once. The rows of `coldata` must be the same samples, in the same order, as the rows of the module matrix (an error is raised otherwise):

- **Numeric traits** are correlated with each module (Spearman by default, `corr_type = "pearson"` for Pearson) and shown in a heatmap, annotated for p-values at or below `pval`. For traits with missing values, each p-value uses the number of samples with both values. Numeric columns are treated as continuous: convert number-coded categories (e.g. a stage coded 1 to 4) to factor to test them as groups.
- **Categorical traits** (text, factor and TRUE/FALSE columns) are tested with one-way ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc tests when `plot_grid = TRUE`, and saved as boxplot grids with one panel per significant module.

Traits that cannot be tested are skipped with a message: numeric traits without variation, and categorical traits with a single level or with one value per sample (e.g. a sample identifier). Use `padj = TRUE` to correct the p-values for multiple testing across the modules, for each trait (Benjamini-Hochberg).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
assoc <- compute.metadata.association(
  scores = res$TF_network[[1]],
  coldata     = traitdata,
  pval        = 0.05,
  file_name   = "Tutorial",
  plot_grid   = TRUE
)

assoc$correlation  # module-trait correlations (numeric traits)
assoc$p_value      # their p-values
assoc$anova        # ANOVA of every module for every categorical trait
```

## **TF modules and pathways**

`compute.modules.relationship()` correlates two matrices of continuous features over the same samples, for example TF modules and pathway activities (Spearman by default, `corr_type = "pearson"` for Pearson), and saves a heatmap of the significant correlations. It is for numeric variables only; use `compute.metadata.association()` for categorical ones. With `plot_grid = TRUE`, a scatter plot is also drawn for the significant pairs (the 100 strongest at most).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rel <- compute.modules.relationship(
  matA      = res$TF_network[[1]],
  matB      = res$Pathways_scores,
  file_name = "Pathways_vs_TF_modules"
)

rel$correlation  # correlations (TF modules x pathways)
rel$p_value      # their p-values
rel$significant  # for each TF module, the pathways significantly correlated with it
```

## **Survival analysis**

`compute.survival.analysis()` compares Kaplan-Meier survival curves with a log-rank test (packages `survival`, `survminer` and `gridExtra`). It works in two modes:

1. **Predefined groups** (`group_column`) — e.g. a clinical risk group or a cluster assignment in the clinical data. Samples without a value for `group_column` are left out.
2. **Feature screening** (`scores`) — e.g. `res$Latent_spaces$Z`. Each feature is split into High/Low at a quantile (`quantile_cutoff`), and the features with a significant log-rank test (`pval`, optionally corrected with `padj = TRUE`) are returned, with a `Statistics` table giving the test of every feature. The rows of `scores` must be the same samples, in the same order, as the rows of the clinical data.

Both modes need a time-to-event column and an event column (1 = event, 0 = censored) in the clinical data. The tutorial `traitdata` includes the overall survival of the patients: `os` (months) and `censOS` (1 = death, 0 = censored).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Predefined groups
surv_group <- compute.survival.analysis(
  coldata       = traitdata,
  time_column   = "os",
  event_column  = "censOS",
  group_column  = "Best.Confirmed.Overall.Response",
  file_name     = "Tutorial"
)

surv_group$p_value     # log-rank p-value
surv_group$median_PFS  # median survival per group (column name kept from the function output)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Feature screening on latent factors
surv_factors <- compute.survival.analysis(
  coldata       = traitdata,
  time_column   = "os",
  event_column  = "censOS",
  scores        = res$Latent_spaces$Z,
  pval          = 0.05,
  quantile_cutoff = 0.5,   # median split; e.g. 0.75 for top quartile vs rest
  file_name     = "Tutorial"

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# Identify TME states (latent factors) in the Gide bulk RNA-seq cohort with CellTFusion
# and relate them to clinical variables (immunotherapy response, therapy, timing).

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(CellTFusion))

work_dir    <- "/home/marcelo.hurtado/Documents/tme_analysis/10d0ef4104/work"
data_dir    <- file.path(work_dir, "data")
results_dir <- file.path(work_dir, "results")
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

## ---- Load data ----------------------------------------------------------

expr <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "Gide_log2TPM.txt"), header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
                    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
coldata_all <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "colData_all.txt"), header = TRUE, sep = " ",
                           quote = "\"", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

coldata <- coldata_all[coldata_all$Cohort == "Gide", ]
rownames(coldata) <- coldata$rna_id

stopifnot(setequal(colnames(expr), rownames(coldata)))
coldata <- coldata[colnames(expr), ]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(expr), rownames(coldata)))

## ---- Back-transform log2(TPM + 1) to linear TPM --------------------------
## CellTFusion(normalized = FALSE) expects TPM-normalized, NOT log-transformed values.
tpm <- 2^as.matrix(expr) - 1
tpm[tpm < 0] <- 0  # clip tiny negative values from floating-point round-trip

cat("Samples:", ncol(tpm), " Genes:", nrow(tpm), "\n")
cat("Response distribution:\n"); print(table(coldata$Response, coldata$Therapy))

## ---- Run CellTFusion pipeline --------------------------------------------

setwd(results_dir)  # package writes its outputs to "Results/" under the working directory

res <- CellTFusion(
  raw_counts     = tpm,
  normalized     = FALSE,
  deconv_methods = c("Quantiseq", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS"),
  do_parallel    = TRUE,
  workers        = 8,
  file_name      = "Gide",
  seed           = 123,
  return         = TRUE,
  verbose        = TRUE
)

saveRDS(res, file.path(results_dir, "CellTFusion_Gide_full_result.rds"))

cat("\n=== Pipeline finished ===\n")
cat("Latent factors (TME states):", ncol(res$Latent_spaces$Z), "\n")
print(colnames(res$Latent_spaces$Z))

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# Identify TME states (latent factors) in the Gide bulk RNA-seq cohort with CellTFusion
# and relate them to clinical variables (immunotherapy response, therapy, timing).

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(CellTFusion))

work_dir    <- "/home/marcelo.hurtado/Documents/tme_analysis/10d0ef4104/work"
data_dir    <- file.path(work_dir, "data")
results_dir <- file.path(work_dir, "results")
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

## ---- Load data ----------------------------------------------------------

expr <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "Gide_log2TPM.txt"), header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
                    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
coldata_all <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "colData_all.txt"), header = TRUE, sep = " ",
                           quote = "\"", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

coldata <- coldata_all[coldata_all$Cohort == "Gide", ]
rownames(coldata) <- coldata$rna_id

stopifnot(setequal(colnames(expr), rownames(coldata)))
coldata <- coldata[colnames(expr), ]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(expr), rownames(coldata)))

## ---- Back-transform log2(TPM + 1) to linear TPM --------------------------
## CellTFusion(normalized = FALSE) expects TPM-normalized, NOT log-transformed values.
tpm <- 2^as.matrix(expr) - 1
tpm[tpm < 0] <- 0  # clip tiny negative values from floating-point round-trip

cat("Samples:", ncol(tpm), " Genes:", nrow(tpm), "\n")
cat("Response distribution:\n"); print(table(coldata$Response, coldata$Therapy))

## ---- Run CellTFusion pipeline --------------------------------------------

setwd(results_dir)  # package writes its outputs to "Results/" under the working directory

  workers        = 8,
  file_name      = "Gide",
  seed           = 123,
  return         = TRUE,
  verbose        = TRUE
)
